---
title: "4 · Quantum Dynamics & Chaos"
---

Random matrix theory characterizes a chaotic spectrum but says nothing about how
information moves in time. This part follows an operator that starts local and
asks how it spreads across the system, the process called scrambling, and
collects the diagnostics that detect it.

The out-of-time-ordered correlator is the primary probe. The squared commutator
$C(t) = \langle |[W(t), V]|^2\rangle$ measures the overlap that an initially
distant operator $W(t)$ develops with a fixed local $V$, and its early growth
defines a quantum Lyapunov exponent bounded by the Maldacena-Shenker-Stanford
inequality $\lambda \le 2\pi k_B T/\hbar$. The spectral form factor reads the same
chaos off the spectrum directly; its dip, ramp, and plateau encode level
repulsion in the time domain, with the plateau height pinned at the
Hilbert-space dimension. Krylov complexity recasts operator growth in a
basis-independent form, mapping the Heisenberg evolution onto a single particle
hopping on a semi-infinite chain whose hopping amplitudes are the Lanczos
coefficients.

It is worth keeping straight what each quantity sees. The squared commutator and
the OTOC are tied by an exact identity at infinite temperature, so operator
growth and a fidelity decay are two readings of one object, whereas the spectral
form factor depends on the spectrum alone and is blind to the choice of operator.

## Notebooks in this part

- [The $C$-$F$ identity](../notebooks/ch4/solution_ch4_commutator_fidelity_identity.ipynb), linking the squared commutator to an OTOC fidelity.
- [The spectral form factor](../notebooks/ch4/solution_ch4_spectral_form_factor_plateau.ipynb), dip, ramp, and the plateau at $K = D$.
- [Krylov complexity](../notebooks/ch4/solution_ch4_krylov_complexity.ipynb), operator growth as a tight-binding chain, with $\mathcal{C}_K(t) = \sinh^2(\alpha t)$.
